proof.criterion: Legion sends no database password to a pod and needs none: the connection a pod uses names the listener in its own container, the credential is obtained there from the pod's own identity, and nothing is written to the pod's disk.
proof.surface: the real agent against a real database through the real proxy: Oh My Pi v18.8.9 (/opt/omp/bin/omp, the worker image's own build), internal/sessionproxy, and PostgreSQL 16.2 reached as the IAM-style login legion-sessions@example-project.iam
proof.command: in an INFRA worker pod: a harness that calls sessionproxy.Start on /tmp/sp/.s.PGSQL.5432 with a dialer that reaches the local PostgreSQL 16.2 at 127.0.0.1:55432, writes ompsessions.Endpoint.AgentURL() into /tmp/sp/OMP_SESSION_SQL_DSN, then runs `/opt/omp/bin/omp gc` with OMP_SESSION_STORAGE=sql and OMP_SESSION_SQL_DSN_FILE naming that file, then reads information_schema.tables back as that login
proof.observed: the file the launcher writes held postgres://legion-sessions%40example-project.iam@localhost/legion_sessions_e2e?path=%2Ftmp%2Fsp%2F.s.PGSQL.5432&sslmode=disable — a login and no password, no credential anywhere else; `omp gc` exited 0; the database then held Oh My Pi's own omp_session_files and omp_session_files_parts, created by the agent through the socket. The upstream saw a plain Postgres startup packet carrying the user and the database and no password, which is what automatic IAM database authentication expects.
proof.negativeControl: the proxy closed and the same command re-run: exit 1 with Oh My Pi's own refusal, `OMP_SESSION_SQL_DSN_FILE names /tmp/sp/OMP_SESSION_SQL_DSN, but the session database could not be opened: Failed to connect (ERR_POSTGRES_CONNECTION_REFUSED)` — the strict open, never a fall back to files

proof.criterion: The listener obtains a credential from the pod's own identity, renews it before it expires, and an agent keeps writing past that expiry with nobody restarting it (the identity source stubbed where the live one is not yet grantable).
proof.surface: the real launcher driving a real child process, its proxy, and a real PostgreSQL 16.2 database, with a dialer that presents a stubbed credential with an expiry at every dial
proof.observed: PASS. One connection through the generation's socket reached the database; the stub's credential then expired and the next connection was refused; a credential minted afresh served the connection after it, through the same running proxy, and the generation's child was still alive (kill -0) throughout. The proxy asks its dialer for a credential at every connection and never pins the first dial's.
proof.negativeControl: the middle connection, made while the stub's credential was expired, failed rather than succeeding — so the test would fail if the dial carried no credential at all

proof.criterion: The listener holds its credential for the generation and nothing between generations, binds its address before the worker starts, and fails the generation loudly rather than starting an agent that would connect to something else.
proof.surface: the real launcher manager with real child processes, real unix sockets and real generation directories on a memory-backed path
proof.observed: PASS, all five. The child reported the socket already bound when it ran; a dialer that refuses made the start refuse with the instance named, with no child started, the generation's directory gone and nothing listening at the path; while a generation ran, its socket was bound and its connection file was 0600 in its own directory, and once the child exited both were gone and a dial of the path was refused, with the next generation getting its own; the connection file was exactly Endpoint.AgentURL() for that generation's directory; a session database named only in part was refused before the launcher started.

proof.criterion: A resume, which opens the same database before the agent starts, works under the same scheme.

trickyParts: The two URL spellings are not interchangeable and both were measured against their real clients in a pod. Oh My Pi hands the DSN file's text to Bun's SQL client (new Bun.SQL(text, {max: 2, idleTimeout: 5}), read out of the image's own binary), which takes a unix socket as the URL's `path` parameter and ignores the host; pgx takes libpq's `host` as the socket's directory and composes .s.PGSQL.5432 itself. ompsessions.Endpoint composes both; a single spelling would have left one of the two clients unable to connect.

The launcher's resume lookup must not read the file it just wrote: that file holds the agent's spelling, which pgx does not parse. start passes the pgx spelling down instead, and the no-session-database path still reads the env pointer exactly as before, retries and all.
writeFiles had to move ahead of the resume lookup, because the lookup is the second database client in the pod and needs the proxy that the generation's directory holds.

The connector's own refresh-ahead certificate cache is library behaviour and is not re-tested here; what the tests prove is that the proxy dials per connection and never pins the first dial's credential.
deviations: The plan's D2 put the agent's endpoint on a loopback port, one per role. The tree's architect asked for a unix socket if the agent's client takes one; it does (measured: Bun's SQL client dials a socket named by the URL's `path` parameter, in Oh My Pi's exact call), so the endpoint is a socket in the generation's own directory on the role container's private volume. It cannot collide with anything the pod binds, and it is reachable only from that role's container rather than from all six. names.go therefore gained no port table and the launcher took three flags rather than four.

The plan's task 8 added a `session-identity` check to scripts/e2e/stage4a-sandbox-runtime.sh. It is not in this branch. The acceptance it was written for was replaced at spec version 3: the live sign-in proof is dispatch://INFRA-320's, which cannot run until dispatch://INFRA-321 gives each project's pods an account of their own. A check that can never run would have shipped unexercised, so it is left to the issue that will run it.

The plan's section 6 expected `a second connection after the first credential's expiry mints a second credential`. The connector does not mint per connection: it keeps a refresh-ahead certificate cache and every dial uses the current credential. The proven property is the one this code owns — a credential per connection, never the first one pinned — and the renewal test is written to that.

CI round: the one-line LEGION_WORKSPACE isolation in the resume-notice test was written by the implementer directly rather than by a deep-worker; the marker-helper fix was a deep-worker's, verified here.
openQuestions: No deployment can run cloudsql-iam until dispatch://INFRA-321 lands: every Legion pod of every project runs as one shared Kubernetes service account, presenting a federated principal with no email address, and Cloud SQL accepts only a user, a service account or a group as a database login. An ADMIN_GCP_TOKEN grant was requested for this issue and approved by the person (request 2753969a-778b-42d2-907d-c0e0345e6047, grant eb11c417-5549-488f-925f-8eaae78a5a87); the tree's architect then ruled the only available route out of scope, because binding or granting that shared account would hand every project's pods the same sign-in. Nothing was applied with the grant — no service account, no binding, no annotation, no Cloud SQL user, no instance flag — and it was revoked unused.

For whoever does apply the instance's identity flag: the Cloud SQL patch replaces the whole databaseFlags list rather than adding to it, so every flag the server already carries must be named in the same patch, and the identity flag itself needs no restart. A read of that instance through ADMIN_GCP_TOKEN is refused HTTP 403 with `Cloud SQL Admin API has not been used in project <credential's project>` — the credential's own project, not the instance's — so such a read needs that API enabled there or an explicit user-project header.
discoveredComplexity: The production proof could be driven here only because a real Postgres could be stood up in the pod without Docker: `uv pip install pgserver` under Python 3.12 carries PostgreSQL 16.2 binaries, and `pg_ctl -o '-h 127.0.0.1 -p 55432'` runs it as the pod's own user. The repository's testpg helper skips every database test without LEGION_TEST_PG_DSN, so that is also how the database-backed launcher tests were run here rather than left to CI.

One test in internal/launcher that predates this branch, TestAResumeIsToldWhetherItsWorkspaceWasRecreatedSinceItsSessionWasWritten, failed when the suite ran inside a Legion pod: the launcher merges os.Environ() into the generation's environment, so the pod's own LEGION_WORKSPACE reached a case written for a child with no workspace. Fixed in the CI round: the test sets LEGION_WORKSPACE empty with t.Setenv.
